newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's communists tell prime minister to quit.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's communists tell prime minister to quit.

text.p: Nepal's opposition communists on Monday urged Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba to resign, saying he had lost his governing majority and should make way for a "clean and transparent" government.

"Deuba should uphold parliamentary morality and democratic norms and resign to make way for a new government," Man Mohan Adhikary, leader of the United Marxist-Leninist (UML) party, told a special session of parliament.
The session was called by King Birendra last week after the communists lodged a no-confidence motion against Deuba's 15-month-old government.
The communists were bolstered by a breakaway faction of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), one of three partners in Deuba's tenuous governing coalition.
Eleven rebel RPP deputies announced last week that they were withdrawing support for Deuba's coalition, which had controlled 108 seats in the 205-seat lower house.
The rebel RPP deputies have accused Deuba's Nepali Congress of harassing their activists and breaking unspecified promises.
To topple Deuba, the opposition would need at least 103 votes as Nepal's constitution requires the motion be passed by a majority of the house.

The speaker of the lower house of parliament, Ram Chandra Poudel, said the no-confidence motion would be debated over three days starting on Saturday and put to a vote after the debate had ended. He did not set a date for the vote.
The government has disputed the opposition's claim that it has the minimum 103 votes to topple Deuba.
Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party has 86 lawmakers. The RPP, considered close to the monarchy, has 19 seats and the third coalition partner, Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP), has three.
The opposition claims the support of at least 102 members -- the UML's 87 deputies, two independents, the 11 rebel RPP deputies and two NSP lawmakers.
But only eight RPP deputies sat with the opposition during Monday's session, which the speaker adjourned after Adhikary's remarks until Saturday.

The Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party (NWPP), a small left-wing group that has three members and potentially holds the swing votes, has not yet committed itself. All three NWPP deputies were absent during Monday's session.

Adhikary became prime minister after his party won general elections in late 1994 and governed until the three opposition parties toppled his minority government and formed a ruling coalition in September 1995.
The communist leader on Monday accused Deuba's coalition of failing to give a sense of direction to the kingdom, one of the world's 10 poorest nations.
He said the government had become a "model of corruption, commission, price rise and unemployment", and said "a clean and transparent government" was needed.
Deuba was present in parliament but did not speak. He was expected to respond to the no-confidence motion next Monday.
